a.explanation: Vincristine causes a dose-dependent peripheral neuropathy (numbness, paresthesias, weakness, areflexia) by disrupting axonal microtubules. Bleomycin causes pulmonary fibrosis, cyclophosphamide hemorrhagic cystitis, doxorubicin cardiotoxicity.

Timolol is a non-selective beta-blocker; ocular absorption can cause bronchospasm in patients with COPD/asthma (the smoker with exertional dyspnea). Apraclonidine, epinephrine and latanoprost do not cause bronchospasm.

SERMs (raloxifene, tamoxifen) increase the risk of venous thromboembolism (DVT/pulmonary embolism) — a key contraindication in patients with prior thrombotic events. They do not cause infections, severe emesis or leukemia.

Paclitaxel (a taxane) binds tubulin and ENHANCES/stabilizes microtubule polymerization, blocking depolymerization → mitotic arrest. Vincristine and vinblastine do the opposite (inhibit polymerization); etoposide and topotecan are topoisomerase inhibitors.

Leucovorin (folinic acid) 'rescues' normal cells from methotrexate's dihydrofolate reductase blockade by providing reduced folate — allowing higher-dose methotrexate therapy (as in osteosarcoma). It does not rescue from cisplatin, doxorubicin or radiotherapy.

Paclitaxel (taxane) is frequently associated with peripheral neuropathy (dose-limiting). Heart failure is doxorubicin's toxicity, hemorrhagic cystitis is cyclophosphamide's, and nephrotoxicity is cisplatin's — but the drug in question here is paclitaxel.

Multidrug resistance is most commonly due to overexpression of P-glycoprotein (MDR1), an ATP-dependent efflux pump that actively transports many anticancer drugs out of the cell. The other mechanisms are less common causes of pleiotropic resistance.

Imatinib is a Bcr-Abl tyrosine kinase inhibitor targeting the Philadelphia chromosome (BCR-ABL fusion) — the treatment of choice for CML. Busulfan and cyclophosphamide are alkylators; trastuzumab targets HER2 in breast cancer.

Doxorubicin (anthracycline) intercalates between DNA base pairs, inhibits topoisomerase II, and generates free radicals via its iron complex → DNA strand breaks and lipid peroxidation. Bleomycin also makes iron-dependent free radicals but does NOT intercalate.

Latanoprost (prostaglandin F2-alpha analogue) is applied once daily (topically) and is first-line for open-angle glaucoma — it increases uveoscleral outflow. Pilocarpine (3-4x/day), carteolol (beta-blocker, bid) and tropicamide (mydriatic) do not match.

Nivolumab (anti-PD-1 checkpoint inhibitor) causes immune-related vitiligo-like depigmentation in melanoma patients. Vemurafenib (BRAF inhibitor) causes photosensitivity; ipilimumab causes colitis/hypophysitis; trametinib (MEK inhibitor) rash.

Tropicamide is an antimuscarinic mydriatic/cycloplegic; pilocarpine, a muscarinic agonist, constricts the pupil (miosis) and reverses the mydriasis and photophobia. Phenylephrine, apraclonidine and timolol do not reverse antimuscarinic mydriasis.

Palmoplantar psoriasis has thick skin — a POTENT topical corticosteroid (betamethasone valerate) is the appropriate initial treatment. Hydrocortisone 1% is too weak; oral prednisolone is avoided in psoriasis (rebound); emollients alone are insufficient.

Vincristine (a vinca alkaloid from the periwinkle plant) causes peripheral neuropathy and alopecia but relatively little myelosuppression or emesis. Cytarabine and etoposide cause significant bone marrow suppression.
Bevacizumab is a monoclonal antibody against VEGF-A that inhibits tumor angiogenesis. Anastrozole and exemestane are aromatase inhibitors; imatinib targets Bcr-Abl/c-KIT.

Busulfan is an alkylating agent (methanesulfonate) classically used for chronic myeloid leukemia (also conditioning for BMT). Imatinib is not an alkylator; cyclophosphamide and dacarbazine are alkylators used for other cancers.

Myelosuppression is the dose-limiting major toxicity of alkylating agents (bone marrow suppression — leucopenia, thrombocytopenia, anemia). Alopecia occurs but is not the major/life-limiting toxicity.

6-MP and 6-TG must be activated by hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HPRT); decreased HPRT activity causes resistance to both (Lesch-Nyhan). Increased DHFR is methotrexate resistance; efflux and polyglutamation apply to other drugs.

Irinotecan is a prodrug activated to SN-38, a topoisomerase I inhibitor; its hallmark toxicity is severe delayed diarrhea (cholinergic + secretory). Vincristine, paclitaxel and docetaxel are not topoisomerase I prodrugs.

a.answer: Drugs more beneficial if major toxicities are non-overlapping
a.explanation: Combination chemotherapy is more effective when agents have non-overlapping toxicities — allowing full doses of each drug. The other statements contradict the principles of combination chemotherapy.

Pityriasis (tinea) versicolor is treated with topical selenium sulphide shampoo (or ketoconazole shampoo/azole creams). Permethrin and benzyl benzoate are for scabies; amphotericin B IV is for systemic mycoses.

Imiquimod (immune response modifier/TLR7 agonist) is used for actinic keratoses, genital warts and superficial BCC — NOT eczema. Urea cream (emollient), tacrolimus ointment (calcineurin inhibitor) and betamethasone (steroid) are all used in eczema.

Bevacizumab is the anti-VEGF monoclonal antibody used (off-label/intravitreal) for neovascular (wet) macular degeneration. Pegaptanib is an anti-VEGF aptamer (not a monoclonal antibody); alemtuzumab and panitumumab are used for other indications.

Cyclosporine binds cyclophilin → inhibits calcineurin → prevents dephosphorylation/activation of NFAT → blocks transcription of IL-2 (and other cytokines) in T cells. Azathioprine and prednisone act via different mechanisms.

Everolimus is an mTOR inhibitor (like sirolimus) — added to calcineurin inhibitor + antimetabolite regimens for synergy. Alemtuzumab is a monoclonal antibody, azathioprine an antimetabolite, tacrolimus a calcineurin inhibitor.

Azathioprine (→6-MP) is activated by TPMT; with TPMT deficiency (or allopurinol inhibiting its metabolism) severe bone marrow suppression occurs — TPMT testing is recommended. The other drugs are not affected by TPMT.

Chronic corticosteroids cause aseptic necrosis of the femoral head, cataracts, hypertension, peptic ulcers, diabetes and osteoporosis — hence the maintenance dose is tapered. Azathioprine, cyclosporine and everolimus are not tapered for these reasons.

Tacrolimus (calcineurin inhibitor) is nephrotoxic — acute and chronic renal impairment — like cyclosporine. It causes hyperglycemia and hyperkalemia (not hypo-), and is not profoundly myelosuppressive.

a.answer: Increased risk of infections and neoplasia
a.explanation: ALL immunosuppressants increase the risk of opportunistic infections and malignancy (especially lymphoproliferative disorders/skin cancer) — the common dose-limiting concern for long-term maintenance. The other side effects are drug-specific.

Bacitracin is a topical polypeptide antibiotic ointment commonly used for blepharitis (eyelid margin infection). Trifluridine is for HSV keratitis, natamycin for fungal keratitis, ciprofloxacin is an ophthalmic solution (drops) rather than the eyelid-margin ointment.

b.modelAnswer:
a) DRUGS IN ABVD (2 marks): A = Adriamycin (doxorubicin); B = Bleomycin; V = Vinblastine; D = Dacarbazine.
b) MODE OF ACTION OF EACH (8 marks):
- Doxorubicin (anthracycline): intercalates between DNA base pairs and inhibits topoisomerase II → DNA strand breaks; also generates free radicals via its iron complex → DNA/membrane damage; inhibits DNA and RNA synthesis.
- Bleomycin: glycopeptide antibiotic that binds DNA and, in the presence of iron and oxygen, generates free radicals → single- and double-strand DNA breaks; cell-cycle specific (G2/M); low myelosuppression.
- Vinblastine (vinca alkaloid): binds tubulin and INHIBITS microtubule polymerization → mitotic (M-phase) arrest; disrupts the mitotic spindle.
- Dacarbazine: alkylating agent — metabolized to a methylating species that methylates DNA (O6-methylguanine) → DNA cross-links/mismatched base pairs → cell death.
c) TWO SIDE EFFECTS OF EACH (8 marks):
- Doxorubicin: cardiotoxicity (cumulative, dose-limiting — heart failure), myelosuppression, alopecia, mucositis, tissue necrosis on extravasation.
- Bleomycin: pulmonary fibrosis (dose-limiting, potentiated by oxygen), skin hyperpigmentation, fever/hypersensitivity reactions, mucositis.
- Vinblastine: myelosuppression (neutropenia — dose-limiting), neurotoxicity (less than vincristine), alopecia, nausea/vomiting.
- Dacarbazine: myelosuppression, severe nausea/vomiting, flu-like syndrome, photosensitivity, local pain at injection site.

TWO TOPICAL DRUGS FOR ACNE (any two) WITH MODE OF ACTION (6 marks):
1. BENZOYL PEROXIDE: antimicrobial — releases reactive oxygen species that kill Cutibacterium (Propionibacterium) acnes; also mildly keratolytic and anti-inflammatory; reduces comedone formation.
2. TRETINOIN (retinoic acid) / ADAPALENE (retinoid): normalizes follicular (epidermal) keratinization and desquamation — comedolytic; unblocks microcomedones; prevents new comedone formation; (adapalene also anti-inflammatory).
3. TOPICAL CLINDAMYCIN (or erythromycin): antibiotic — inhibits bacterial (C. acnes) protein synthesis at the 50S ribosomal subunit → reduces colonization and inflammation.
4. AZELAIC ACID: antimicrobial against C. acnes and normalizes keratinization (comedolytic).
5. SALICYLIC ACID: keratolytic — loosens comedones.
(Any two well-described drugs; marks for drug + mode of action.)

APRACLONIDINE vs PILOCARPINE (4 marks):
APRACLONIDINE (alpha-2 adrenergic agonist): DECREASES AQUEOUS HUMOR PRODUCTION — activates alpha-2 receptors on the ciliary epithelium → reduced cAMP → less aqueous secretion → lower intraocular pressure (IOP). It causes minimal miosis and works independently of the outflow pathway.
PILOCARPINE (muscarinic/cholinergic agonist): INCREASES AQUEOUS HUMOR OUTFLOW — stimulates M3 muscarinic receptors → contraction of the ciliary muscle → pulls the scleral spur, opening the trabecular meshwork → increased conventional outflow → lower IOP; also causes miosis (contraction of the iris sphincter).
COMPARISON/CONTRAST: both lower IOP in open-angle glaucoma, but apraclonidine reduces aqueous production while pilocarpine increases aqueous drainage; apraclonidine causes mydriasis-minimal changes and may be used as an adjunct, whereas pilocarpine causes marked miosis and accommodative spasm (blurred vision); pilocarpine is contraindicated in narrow-angle glaucoma (can precipitate angle closure), apraclonidine has fewer accommodative effects.

MODE OF ACTION OF THE IMMUNOSUPPRESSANTS (6 marks):
a) SIROLIMUS (rapamycin): binds the intracellular immunophilin FKBP12 → the complex inhibits mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) → blocks IL-2 (and other cytokine)-driven signal transduction → arrests T-cell proliferation in G1 phase (does not inhibit calcineurin).
b) AZATHIOPRINE: prodrug converted to 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP) → inhibits de novo purine synthesis (and incorporates into DNA) → reduces lymphocyte (T- and B-cell) proliferation.
c) MYCOPHENOLATE MOFETIL: prodrug hydrolyzed to mycophenolic acid → selectively and reversibly inhibits inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase (IMPDH) → blocks de novo guanine nucleotide synthesis (lymphocytes depend on this pathway) → inhibits T- and B-cell proliferation.

CHECKPOINT INHIBITORS (6 marks):
a) THREE CLASSES WITH ONE EXAMPLE EACH:
1. Anti-CTLA-4 antibodies — Ipilimumab.
2. Anti-PD-1 antibodies — Nivolumab (or pembrolizumab).
3. Anti-PD-L1 antibodies — Atezolizumab (or durvalumab, avelumab).
[These remove the brakes on T cells: CTLA-4 blockade enhances T-cell priming in lymphoid tissue; PD-1/PD-L1 blockade reinvigorates exhausted T cells in the tumor microenvironment → anti-tumor immunity.]
b) TWO SIDE EFFECTS OF EACH (immune-related adverse events):
- Ipilimumab: immune-mediated colitis (diarrhea), dermatitis/rash; hepatitis, hypophysitis/endocrinopathies.
- Nivolumab: pneumonitis, thyroiditis/hypothyroidism; colitis, hepatitis, dermatitis.
- Atezolizumab: pneumonitis, hepatitis; colitis, fatigue, infusion reactions.
(Any two per drug.)

c.modelAnswer:
HER-2 POSITIVE BREAST CANCER — CMF + TRASTUZUMAB:
a) MODE OF ACTION (8 marks):
- Cyclophosphamide: alkylating agent — activated in the liver to phosphoramide mustard → alkylates/cross-links DNA strands → blocks DNA replication → cell death (cell-cycle non-specific).
- Methotrexate: antifolate antimetabolite — inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) → depletes tetrahydrofolate → blocks thymidylate and purine synthesis → inhibits DNA synthesis (S-phase specific).
- 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU): antimetabolite — converted to 5-FdUMP, which irreversibly inhibits thymidylate synthase → blocks thymidylate synthesis → inhibits DNA synthesis (S-phase specific).
- Trastuzumab: humanized monoclonal antibody against the HER2/neu (ErbB2) receptor — binds the extracellular domain → blocks HER2 signaling, down-regulates the receptor, and triggers antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) against HER2-overexpressing tumor cells.
b) REASONS FOR MESNA AND LEUCOVORIN (3 marks):
- MESNA: inactivates acrolein, the urotoxic metabolite of cyclophosphamide, in the urinary tract → prevents hemorrhagic cystitis (given with high-dose cyclophosphamide).
- LEUCOVORIN (folinic acid): 'rescue' therapy — provides reduced folate that bypasses the methotrexate-induced DHFR blockade, rescuing normal (and tumor) cells; also enhances 5-FU cytotoxicity by stabilizing the ternary complex of thymidylate synthase.
c) IF HER2-NEGATIVE (2 marks): Trastuzumab would NOT be prescribed — there is no HER2 receptor over-expression/target for the antibody to bind, so it would have no therapeutic effect.
d) IF ER-POSITIVE (1 + 1 marks):
i) Add TAMOXIFEN (a selective estrogen receptor modulator) — or an aromatase inhibitor (e.g., anastrozole) in post-menopausal women.
ii) Reason: ER-positive breast cancer growth is driven by estrogen; tamoxifen blocks estrogen receptors on tumor cells → inhibits estrogen-stimulated proliferation → reduces recurrence and mortality.

ATROPINE FOR FUNDOSCOPIC EXAMINATION:
a) MODE OF ACTION (2 marks): Atropine is a competitive muscarinic (anticholinergic) receptor antagonist. In the eye it blocks M3 receptors on the iris sphincter pupillae → MYDRIASIS (pupil dilatation), and on the ciliary muscle → CYCLOPLEGIA (paralysis of accommodation) — allowing full examination of the fundus.
b) FOUR OTHER DRUGS FOR FUNDOSCOPY (4 marks): Tropicamide; Cyclopentolate; Homatropine; Phenylephrine (alpha-1 adrenergic agonist — mydriatic only, no cycloplegia). (Any four.)
c) SIX OTHER CLINICAL APPLICATIONS OF ATROPINE (6 marks):
1. Pre-anaesthetic medication — reduces salivary/bronchial secretions (antisialagogue) and prevents vagal bradycardia.
2. Treatment of bradyarrhythmias — sinus bradycardia and AV block (IV atropine).
3. Antidote for organophosphate/anticholinesterase poisoning (with pralidoxime).
4. Antidote for cholinergic excess/mushroom poisoning (muscarine).
5. Antispasmodic in gastrointestinal disorders — peptic ulcer, irritable bowel (reduces motility and secretion).
6. Bronchodilation in asthma/COPD (though inhaled ipratropium is preferred).
7. Uveitis/iritis — mydriasis and cycloplegia prevent posterior synechiae formation.
8. Urinary incontinence/overactive bladder — antispasmodic effect on the detrusor. (Any six.)
d) SIX SIDE EFFECTS OF ATROPINE (3 marks): Dry mouth (xerostomia); blurred vision (cycloplegia); photophobia; tachycardia; urinary retention; constipation; dry/flushed skin with hyperthermia (anhidrosis); CNS effects — restlessness, confusion, hallucinations (central anticholinergic syndrome). (Any six.)
